section.title: Spiritual Blessings in Christ
section.sectionRationale: This is the doorway into the whole letter, one long sentence in the Greek that pours out praise for what the triune God has done in Christ. Before Paul says a single word about how the church should live, he floods the reader with grace: the Father chose and adopted us, the Son redeemed us by His blood, and the Spirit sealed us as a pledge of what is still to come. Everything the rest of Ephesians asks of us flows from this opening flood of blessing.
section.thesis: The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in Christ, choosing and adopting us before the foundation of the world, redeeming us through the blood of the Son, and sealing us with the Holy Spirit as the pledge of our inheritance, all of it to the praise of His glorious grace.
section.frameNote: Four movements shaped by the Trinity: the greeting from Paul to the saints; the Father who chose and adopted us in love; the Son in whom we have redemption and the gathering up of all things; and the Spirit who seals us and guarantees our inheritance.

units.label: Greeting
units.note: grace and peace to the saints

verses.text: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, To the saints in Ephesus, the faithful in Christ Jesus:
Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

units.label: Chosen and adopted by the Father
units.note: before the foundation of the world

verses.text: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual {{eulogia|blessing}} in the heavenly realms.
For He {{eklegomai|chose}} us in Him before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless in His presence. In love
He {{proorizo|predestined}} us for {{huiothesia|adoption}} as His sons through Jesus Christ, according to the good pleasure of His will,
to the praise of His glorious grace, which He has freely given us in the Beloved One.

units.label: Redeemed in the Son
units.note: forgiveness and the gathering of all things

verses.text: In Him we have {{apolutrosis|redemption}} through His blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of His grace
that He lavished on us with all wisdom and understanding.
And He has made known to us the {{mysterion|mystery}} of His will according to His good pleasure, which He purposed in Christ
as a plan for the fullness of time, to bring all things in heaven and on earth {{anakephalaioo|together}} in Christ.
In Him we were also chosen as God's own, having been predestined according to the plan of Him who works out everything by the counsel of His will,
in order that we, who were the first to hope in Christ, would be for the praise of His glory.
And in Him, having heard and believed the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, you were {{sphragizo|sealed}} with the promised Holy Spirit,
who is the {{arrabon|pledge}} of our inheritance until the redemption of those who are God's possession, to the praise of His glory.

eulogia.gloss: Blessing, a good word spoken and the good gift it conveys. The related verb runs three times through verse 3: the God who is blessed has blessed us with every blessing. These are spiritual blessings in the heavenly realms, not primarily earthly comforts but the whole treasure of salvation already ours in Christ, election, adoption, redemption, the sealing Spirit, and the inheritance to come.

eklegomai.gloss: To choose out, to select for oneself. God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world, so that election is grounded in His own free love and purpose rather than in anything He foresaw in us. The goal of the choosing is stated at once: that we should be holy and blameless in His presence.

proorizo.gloss: To mark out beforehand, to determine in advance. Paul says God predestined us for adoption according to the good pleasure of His will. The word stresses God's prior, purposeful decision, and Paul always frames it in Christ and toward a goal, sonship and the praise of God's glory, never as cold fate.

huiothesia.gloss: Adoption as sons, the legal placing of an outsider into the full status and inheritance of a child. In the Roman world an adopted son gained the family name, rights, and estate. God predestined us for this: not merely forgiven servants but sons and heirs, brought into His family through Jesus Christ.

apolutrosis.gloss: Redemption, release secured by the payment of a ransom, the language of buying a slave or captive into freedom. In Christ this redemption comes through His blood and is defined at once as the forgiveness of our trespasses. The same word returns in verse 14 for the final redemption of God's possession, the completion of what the cross began.

mysterion.gloss: Mystery, a purpose once hidden in God and now openly revealed. It is not a riddle to be solved but a secret God has disclosed: His plan to sum up all things in Christ. Later in Ephesians the mystery includes Jew and Gentile made one in Christ, the unfolding of this single saving purpose.

anakephalaioo.gloss: To sum up, to bring together under one head. God's plan for the fullness of time is to gather all things in heaven and on earth into unity under Christ as head. The shattered cosmos, fractured by sin, is to be reunited and reordered in the Son, the goal toward which all history moves.

sphragizo.gloss: To seal, to stamp with a mark of ownership, authenticity, and protection. When they believed, God sealed the Ephesians with the promised Holy Spirit, marking them as His own and securing them until the day of redemption. The seal is not a thing but a Person, the Spirit Himself given to God's people.

arrabon.gloss: A pledge, deposit, or down payment that guarantees the full amount will follow. The Holy Spirit is God's first installment of the inheritance, a real foretaste that secures the whole. In later Greek the same word came to mean an engagement ring, a fitting picture of the Spirit as God's binding promise of the glory to come.

basic.context: Ephesians opens not with a problem to fix but with praise to pour out. In one long, breathless sentence Paul blesses God for every blessing He has given us in Christ. He traces salvation through the whole Trinity: the Father chose and adopted us before the world began, the Son redeemed us by His blood and forgives our sins, and the Spirit seals us as God's own and guarantees the inheritance still to come. All of it is to the praise of God's glorious grace.
basic.hermeneutics: This is worship before it is teaching. Paul is not laying out a cold system but overflowing with gratitude, and the doctrines of election, adoption, and redemption come to us wrapped in praise. Notice the refrain, to the praise of His glory, marking off the Father's, the Son's, and the Spirit's work. Read it first as a hymn of thanks for what God has done, and only then as a map of how He saves.
basic.originalLanguages: The passage turns on rich words. God has blessed us with every eulogia, spiritual blessing. He eklegomai, chose, us in Christ before the foundation of the world, and proorizo, predestined, us for huiothesia, adoption as sons. In the Son we have apolutrosis, redemption, through His blood. God made known the mysterion, the once hidden purpose, to anakephalaioo, to sum up, all things in Christ. And the Spirit sphragizo, seals, us, given as the arrabon, the pledge, of our inheritance.
basic.typology: Redemption through blood recalls the Passover and the whole sacrificial system, where a life was given so God's people could go free, now fulfilled in the blood of Christ. Adoption as sons takes up Israel's calling as God's son and opens it to all who are in Christ. The sealing Spirit answers the long promise of the Spirit poured out in the last days, given now as the first fruits of the age to come.
basic.christ: Everything here happens in Christ, in Him, through Him. He is the Beloved One in whom the Father freely gives us grace, the one through whose blood we are redeemed and forgiven, the head under whom all things in heaven and earth will be gathered. The Father chose us in Him before the world began, and it is by belonging to Christ that we receive every spiritual blessing.
basic.god: The Father is the fountain of all this grace, blessing, choosing, adopting, and working out everything by the counsel of His will. He is a God of purpose and of lavish generosity, who plans salvation before creation and pours it out at the fullness of time. And He does it all to the praise of His glorious grace, so that His goodness is displayed and enjoyed forever.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 8 speaks of those God foreknew and predestined, adopted as sons and given the Spirit as first fruits. 2 Corinthians 1 calls the Spirit God's seal and pledge in our hearts. Colossians 1 names the redemption and forgiveness we have in the beloved Son.
basic.oneStory: This passage lifts the curtain on God's plan from before creation to the fullness of time. What was fractured at the fall is being gathered up again in Christ, all things in heaven and on earth summed up under one head. The Ephesians, and every believer, are caught up into that plan, chosen, redeemed, and sealed, a down payment on the day when the whole cosmos finds its unity in the Son.

context.literary:
Ephesians 1:3 to 14 is a single sentence in the Greek, a rolling chain of relative clauses and participles that runs for twelve verses without a full stop. English versions break it up, but the original asks to be heard in one breath. Its form is that of a Jewish blessing, a berakah, the kind of prayer that begins 'Blessed be God' and then recites what God has done. Paul then arranges the recital around the three persons of the Trinity: the Father chooses and adopts in verses 3 to 6, the Son redeems and reveals in verses 7 to 12, the Spirit seals in verses 13 and 14. Each movement closes on a refrain, 'to the praise of His glorious grace,' verse 6, 'for the praise of His glory,' verse 12, and again in verse 14.

Two devices hold the sentence together. The first is the constant phrase 'in Christ,' with its variants 'in Him' and 'in the Beloved One,' which recurs through the passage until it becomes the grammar of the whole. Nothing is given to us apart from Him. The second is a sweep of time. The sentence starts before the foundation of the world, verse 4, passes to the cross in verse 7, looks to 'the fullness of time' in verse 10, and ends on the inheritance still to come, verse 14. Beginning, middle and end are all held inside one sentence.

The letter's opening also bears a small textual note. Some of the earliest manuscripts lack the words 'in Ephesus' in verse 1, which has led many to think the letter was a circular for several churches. That does not alter the passage, which reads as addressed to saints everywhere, and it explains the general, doctrinal tone that follows.
context.historical:
Paul writes as 'an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God,' and he writes from prison, as Ephesians 3:1 and 6:20 make clear. The city of Ephesus was the great port and temple city of Roman Asia, home of the temple of Artemis, a place of magic and civic cults, and the church there was a mixed company of Jews and Gentiles. Acts 19 describes Paul's long ministry there and the collapse of the trade in magic books. Hearing a long praise of the God who chose and adopted them would have been an answer to a world of powers and fates, where religion was a matter of appeasing hostile forces.

The vocabulary would have rung in two directions. For Jewish readers the language of choice and sonship recalled Israel: 'The LORD your God has chosen you to be a people for His prized possession,' Deuteronomy 7:6, and 'Israel is My firstborn son,' Exodus 4:22. For Gentile readers, adoption was a familiar legal act in Roman life, by which someone outside a family was taken in as a son with the full standing of an heir. Paul uses both pictures at once and then tells the Gentiles that what Israel was given has come to them as well. The words 'we who were the first to hope in Christ,' verse 12, and 'you also,' verse 13, show him moving from Jewish believers to Gentile believers inside a single sentence. That movement is the background to the whole letter, which deals with the union of the two groups.

The sealing language would also have been understood. A seal marked ownership and authenticity on documents and goods, and the word for a pledge was used in commercial dealings for a first payment that guaranteed the rest. Paul draws on a world where people knew what a down payment was.
context.canonical:
The blessing of verse 3 stands in a long line of Scripture's praise. 'Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ' opens 2 Corinthians 1:3 and 1 Peter 1:3 in almost the same words, and the pattern goes back to the Psalms, which close their books with 'Blessed be the LORD,' for example Psalm 41:13 and Psalm 72:18. Paul's innovation is to name God as Father of the Lord Jesus Christ and to bless Him for what He has done in Christ.

The theme of choice reaches back to the Old Testament in several steps. God chose Abraham, Nehemiah 9:7, and then Israel, Deuteronomy 7:6 to 8, which says explicitly that it was not because they were many but because the LORD loved them. Paul says the same pattern now covers those in Christ. Adoption echoes Exodus 4:22 and Hosea 11:1. The redemption of verse 7 recalls the exodus, where God redeemed His people from slavery, and Isaiah, where the Redeemer buys back His own.

The mystery of verse 9 draws on Daniel 2, where God reveals what was hidden, and Paul's use of 'mystery' throughout the letter, Ephesians 3:3 to 6, shows that it refers to what the prophets glimpsed but did not see fully.

Forward from here, Romans 8:29 and 30 gives the same chain of purpose, 2 Corinthians 1:22 gives the same seal and pledge, Colossians 1:13 and 14 gives the same redemption and forgiveness, and 1 Peter 1:1 to 5 stands very close, with chosen, sanctified, inheritance and praise to the God and Father. Revelation closes the story with the inheritance fully received, Revelation 21:7.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul does not open this letter with a problem to solve. He opens by lifting the eyes of believers to the largest view he can give them, so that the rest of the letter, with its demands about unity and holy living, can be heard from inside it. Most of the churches Paul wrote to were wrestling with a particular failure. Here he wants the readers to know what is true of them before he asks anything of them. Every instruction in chapters 4 to 6 rests on this.

He also means these truths to produce humility and security together. Election, adoption and the seal are listed in a sentence that never mentions human merit. The only things that stand on the human side are hearing and believing, verse 13. A believer who is anxious about standing with God is told that the Father chose them before they existed, the Son bought them with His blood, and the Spirit has marked them as His own. A believer who is proud is told there is nothing here to boast about. And a believer who is tempted to think the church is only a human society is told that it was planned in eternity and is aimed at the summing up of all things.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Almost everything in this passage describes what God has done, not what believers must do. 'He chose us,' 'He predestined us,' 'we have redemption,' 'you were sealed' are statements of accomplished fact, offered as ground for praise, not as a to do list. The only command-like element is the form of the whole: it is a blessing, and the reader joins in by blessing God too.

That matters for how we apply it. These verses are not a manual for deciding who is or is not elect, and they are not a basis for speculation about other people's destiny. Paul speaks of 'us' who are in Christ, and he writes to encourage those who already believe. Applying the text rightly means taking comfort from it, giving thanks, and letting it ground the call to holiness that follows in the letter. The goal of election in verse 4 is that we should be 'holy and blameless,' so the doctrine is not a licence for carelessness but its opposite.

debates.question: What does it mean that God chose us 'in Him' before the foundation of the world?

views.label: God chose particular individuals in Christ
views.case: The verbs are aimed at persons: 'He chose us,' 'He predestined us,' and 'chosen as God's own... according to the plan of Him who works out everything by the counsel of His will,' verse 11. Romans 8:29 and 30 and Romans 9:11 to 16 speak of God's purpose and calling, not human decision, as the cause of salvation. Augustine and the Reformers, Calvin above all, read the passage this way, with 'in Christ' naming the one in whom the elect are chosen and saved.

views.label: God chose the people, the church, in Christ, and individuals share in it by faith
views.case: Paul says 'in Him,' and the chosen body is the one found in Christ. Those in Christ are the elect, so a person enters the chosen people by being united to Him through faith, verse 13. On this reading the emphasis lies on God choosing a people with a purpose, to be holy and blameless, as He chose Israel, not on a list of names. Many Arminian and some Lutheran interpreters hold this.

views.label: God chose on the basis of foreknown faith
views.case: Appeal is made to 1 Peter 1:2, 'chosen according to the foreknowledge of God,' and to Romans 8:29, 'those God foreknew.' The thought is that God foresaw who would believe and chose them in Christ.

debates.bearing: Paul's own purpose in the sentence is to move readers to praise and security, not to settle this question. On every view the choice is in Christ, springs from love, aims at holiness, and leaves nothing for human boasting. Care is needed to avoid reading one's preferred system into a hymn.

debates.question: What does 'sealed with the promised Holy Spirit' refer to?

views.label: The gift of the Spirit received at conversion
views.case: The participle 'having believed' and the verb 'were sealed' are linked, and Paul speaks to all his readers. Romans 8:9 says anyone without the Spirit of Christ does not belong to Him. The seal is the Spirit Himself, given to every believer when they believe, as in 2 Corinthians 1:22.

views.label: A second experience after conversion
views.case: Some have read the sequence 'having believed... you were sealed' as pointing to a later event, and have connected it to episodes in Acts such as Acts 19:2 where believers received the Spirit afterwards. The seal is then a special empowering.

views.label: Baptism as the sign of the seal
views.case: A number of church traditions connect the seal with baptism, as the outward sign marking God's ownership, with the Spirit as the one who gives what the sign signifies.

debates.bearing: The text says the Spirit is the seal and is given to those who heard and believed. The surrounding verses speak of every believer, which fits the first view best, and Ephesians 4:30 warns all the readers not to grieve the Spirit by whom they were sealed.

study.originalLanguages:
The vocabulary the basic study names is only part of this sentence. Several other words carry weight.

Start with eudokia, 'good pleasure,' in verses 5 and 9. The word names what God is pleased to do, His delight and favour, and not mere permission or calculation. Paul uses it twice, once for adoption and once for the revealed mystery, so that both are done out of God's own gladness. The same word stands at the heart of the voice at Jesus' baptism, 'in whom I am well pleased,' Matthew 3:17, which connects the Father's delight in the Son with His delight in adopting those in Him.

Next, the phrase translated 'freely given' in verse 6 is a verb built on charis, grace. It means roughly 'graced us with grace,' a doubled expression that the English has to smooth out. The favour is not only offered; it is bestowed, and bestowed 'in the Beloved One,' a title for the Son that recalls the Father's words in the Gospels.

In verse 8 the verb for 'lavished' is perisseuo, which means to overflow, to be in excess. The picture is of a container that cannot hold what is poured into it. It appears with the word 'riches' in verse 7, so that grace is described as measured by wealth and delivered with excess.

The word rendered 'plan' in verse 10 is oikonomia, the management of a household. It is the root of our word economy. God is pictured as the manager of a household who arranges the right moments for the right things. The 'fullness of time' is the point at which He brings everything under one head. The same word appears again in Ephesians 3:2 and 3:9.

In verse 11 the verb translated 'chosen as God's own' is from a root associated with a lot or an inheritance. The same word group underlies kleronomia, inheritance, in verses 14 and 18. The wording can be read as 'we were made an inheritance,' so that believers are both heirs and God's own portion. The footnote in many Bibles shows this alternative, and the word fits Deuteronomy 32:9, where the LORD's people are His portion.

Finally, the word 'heavenly realms' in verse 3 is epouranios, a single adjective Paul uses five times in this letter, here and in Ephesians 1:20, 2:6, 3:10 and 6:12. It names the sphere where Christ reigns, where believers are already seated, and where hostile powers still operate. The blessing is said to be located there, which means it is secure, out of the reach of earthly loss.

typology.type: Israel as God's chosen son and treasured possession
typology.fulfillment: Israel was chosen, not for size, but because the LORD loved them, Deuteronomy 7:6 to 8, and was called 'My firstborn son,' Exodus 4:22. Paul takes the same pattern of free election and sonship and says it now takes in all who are in Christ, Jew and Gentile. The one true Son, Jesus, is the Beloved in whom the choice is made. Israel's history of exile shows where the type fell short: the nation was chosen but could not keep the covenant, whereas those chosen in Christ are held by Him, Romans 8:30.

The exodus was a redemption by a mighty hand, a purchase out of slavery, Deuteronomy 7:8. Paul's 'redemption through His blood' in verse 7 takes the same picture and gives it a price. The Passover lamb's blood marked the houses spared, Exodus 12:13, and Christ's blood does the larger thing, 1 Peter 1:18 and 19. The exodus freed one people from one oppressor, while this redemption frees from sin and its penalty. The type falls short because the exodus generation still died in the wilderness, whereas the redeemed in Christ receive an inheritance that does not perish, 1 Peter 1:4.

Israel's land was an inheritance given by promise, and the people were themselves the LORD's portion, Deuteronomy 32:9. Paul speaks of an inheritance, verse 14, and of believers as God's own, verse 11. The land becomes the new heavens and earth, and the Spirit is the pledge of arrival. The land was lost through exile, and the type points beyond itself to a place no one can lose, Hebrews 11:16.

Ownership marks and first installments belonged to ordinary life and to the temple, where offerings were set apart for God, as in Exodus 28:36 on the plate marked 'Holy to the LORD.' The Spirit given to believers is the mark of belonging to God and the first payment of the full inheritance. 2 Corinthians 1:22 and 5:5 say the same. What the type could only show by an external sign, the Spirit does from within. It remains a pledge, not the whole, because creation still waits, Romans 8:23.

study.christ:
The first thing to see is the repetition. 'In Christ,' 'in Him,' 'in the Beloved One' run through these verses like a drumbeat. Paul does not say that God gave good things and Christ helped. He says every blessing is located in Christ, so that to be without Him is to be without them. We were chosen in Him before the world began, verse 4, which means that Christ is not an afterthought to some earlier plan. He is the plan's centre before anything was made. Colossians 1:16 says all things were created through Him and for Him, and Ephesians 1 supplies the other half, that all things will be gathered up in Him.

Second, He is the Beloved. The title carries the Father's love for the Son, as at His baptism, Matthew 3:17. Grace is freely given to us 'in the Beloved One.' The love the Father has for His Son is the love poured out on those joined to Him, which is the heart of Jesus' prayer in John 17:23 and 17:26. We are not loved at a distance but within the love between Father and Son.

Third, He is the Redeemer, and the price is named: 'through His blood.' Everything abstract in the sentence, choice and predestination and adoption, rests on that concrete event at the cross. Adoption is 'through Jesus Christ,' verse 5. Forgiveness is not an act of overlooking, it is an act of purchase, Revelation 5:9. Paul has already made the point in Galatians 4:4 and 4:5, that God sent His Son to redeem those under the law so that we might receive adoption.

Fourth, He is the one to whom everything is heading. Verse 10 says God's purpose is 'to bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ.' The verb behind it means to gather under a single head, and the head is Christ, as the next paragraph says, Ephesians 1:22. The divisions of the universe, between heaven and earth, between Jew and Gentile, between God and humanity, are healed in Him. Ephesians 2:14 to 16 is the follow through.

Fifth, He is the one the Spirit seals us into. The Spirit is 'the Spirit of His Son,' Galatians 4:6, and the sealing is the way Christ's own life is given to believers. Romans 8:9 says the Spirit is the Spirit of Christ.

Last, it is worth avoiding forced allegory. The 'mystery' of verse 9 is not a code for the cross hidden in the Old Testament stories; Paul says plainly that the mystery is the plan to unite all things in Christ, and Ephesians 3:4 to 6 says the Gentiles being fellow heirs is part of it. The links to Christ here are stated by Paul himself, not discovered by guesswork.
study.god:
This is the most concentrated statement of God's purpose in the New Testament, and several things stand out about the God it describes.

He is a God who plans. The verbs of verses 4, 5, 9 and 11 are about forethought: He chose, He predestined, He purposed, He works out everything by the counsel of His will. Nothing in salvation is improvised. A God who plans before creation is not caught off guard by the fall or by any later disaster. For believers, this is the ground of deep security. Romans 8:28 says that God works all things together for the good of those who love Him, and this passage supplies the reason why.

He is a God of love. Verse 4 ends with 'In love' and the clause that follows, verse 5, is anchored in it. Some translations attach those words to being 'holy and blameless in His presence in love,' while others attach them to 'He predestined us in love.' Either way the decision to adopt rests on love, not on any attractiveness in the adopted. Deuteronomy 7:7 and 8 makes the same point about Israel. The Father's love is the source, not the response.

He is a God who gives with excess. The words riches, lavished, and freely given repeat the same message. God does not ration grace. He pours it out 'with all wisdom and understanding,' verse 8, meaning that this generosity is also not careless, it is intelligent and ordered toward a purpose.

He is a God whose sovereignty and goodness are not in tension in this text. He 'works out everything by the counsel of His will,' verse 11, and yet the will is called 'good pleasure,' the gladness of a Father. Paul does not defend this sovereignty against objections here, he praises it. The related questions about human responsibility are taken up elsewhere, such as Romans 9, and in this letter's insistence on faith, verse 13, and on a life of good works, Ephesians 2:10.

He is a Trinitarian God, and the passage is one of the clearest examples of the three persons working as one purpose. The Father chooses, the Son redeems, the Spirit seals, and each work is for 'the praise of His glory.' It is also notable that this is no cold doctrine of God but a doctrine that makes Paul break into praise.

The result for worship is that the proper first response is not argument but blessing. The passage itself models this by being a blessing. The God who is blessed is the God who has blessed us, and the only fitting answer to a gift of this size is thanks that does not stop.

crossReferences.note: Paul gives the same chain of purpose here as in Ephesians 1: foreknown, predestined, called, justified, glorified. The goal is to be 'conformed to the image of His Son,' which matches 'holy and blameless' and adoption in verses 4 and 5. It shows that the chain ends in glory.

God chose Israel not because they were many, but because He loved them and kept His oath. This is the Old Testament pattern behind Paul's language of choice, showing that the root of election is the Lord's love and not human worth.

God sent His Son to redeem those under the law so that we could receive adoption, and sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts crying 'Abba, Father.' It lines up with verses 5 to 7 and 13 to 14: adoption, redemption and the Spirit arrive together.

Another blessing that opens with 'Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,' and then lists new birth, a living hope, and an imperishable inheritance reserved in heaven. It shares both the opening and the forward looking inheritance of verse 14.
Every promise of God finds its 'Yes' in Christ, and God sets His seal on us and gives the Spirit in our hearts as a pledge. It is the closest parallel to the seal and pledge of verses 13 and 14.

Christ is the image of the invisible God, creator of all things, head of the body, and the one through whom God reconciles all things, whether on earth or in heaven. This is the large background for verse 10, the gathering of all things in Christ.

The Spirit of sonship lets us cry 'Abba, Father,' and makes us heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ. It explains how adoption in verse 5 becomes an experienced reality, and ties sonship to the inheritance of verse 14.
Jesus prays that the world may know the Father loved those in Christ even as He loved the Son. It supports reading 'the Beloved One' as the place where the Father's love reaches us.

Believers are told not to grieve the Holy Spirit 'in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.' This ties the seal of 1:13 to ongoing life and shows that the seal lasts until redemption is complete.

'The one who overcomes will inherit all things, and I will be his God, and he will be My son.' The language of inheritance and sonship from Ephesians 1:5 and 1:14 arrives at its completion in the new creation.

study.oneStory:
Ephesians 1:3 to 14 sits at a vantage point from which the whole biblical story can be seen. The Bible begins with a creation in which humanity is made to live before God, then shows how that was lost. This passage tells us the rescue was not a reaction. 'Before the foundation of the world,' verse 4, God had already purposed to have a people in Christ. The fall did not surprise Him, and the story of redemption is the unfolding of a plan older than the story of sin.

What does it answer from before? It answers the question of why God would bother with Israel and then with the nations. The call of Abraham, the exodus, the covenant, the exile and the return are all moves within a purpose already set. Israel's election was real, and it was meant for the blessing of the nations, Genesis 12:3. Paul says that blessing has come in Christ, with 'every spiritual blessing,' and that the promised Spirit has been poured out, as the prophets said, Joel 2:28 and Ezekiel 36:27.

What does it set up? The rest of the letter. Chapter 2 shows Jew and Gentile made one, chapter 3 explains the mystery now revealed, and chapters 4 to 6 describe the life of a people chosen to be holy and blameless. The church is not an accident; it is the visible form of the purpose in verse 10, the first fruit of a gathered universe. Believers live in the time between the first payment and the full inheritance, sealed, assured, and still waiting, Romans 8:23.

How does it end? The sentence ends where the Bible ends, with inheritance and praise. 'Until the redemption of those who are God's possession' points to the day when God's people receive what they have been promised, and Revelation 21:1 to 7 describes the new heaven and earth where God dwells with His people and they are His sons and daughters. Then what verse 10 promised, all things in heaven and on earth gathered together in Christ, will be visible fact. And the praise that Paul keeps repeating, 'to the praise of His glory,' will be the sound of the whole creation.

quiz.q: Where and in whom are the blessings of this passage found?

options.text: In Christ, every spiritual blessing in the heavenly realms.
options.note: The phrase in Christ, or in Him, runs through the whole passage as the sphere of blessing.

options.text: In our own effort to earn God's favor.
options.note: The blessings are freely given in the Beloved One, not earned.

options.text: Mainly in earthly wealth and comfort.
options.note: These are spiritual blessings in the heavenly realms, the treasures of salvation.

options.text: In the spiritual powers Ephesus feared.
options.note: Christ is above every power; the blessings are in Him alone.

quiz.q: When did God choose His people, according to verse 4?

options.text: Before the foundation of the world.
options.note: Election is grounded in God's eternal purpose, before creation.

options.text: After He saw that they would believe on their own.
options.note: A view some hold, but Paul roots the choice in the good pleasure of His will.

options.text: At the moment they were baptized.
options.note: The choosing is before the world's foundation, not at a later ritual.

options.text: God did not choose; it was all human decision.
options.note: The text plainly says He chose us in Him.

quiz.q: What does adoption as sons mean here?

options.text: God places us into His family with the full status and inheritance of children.
options.note: Adoption, huiothesia, grants the name, rights, and inheritance of a son.

options.text: We become servants who hope one day to earn a place.
options.note: Adoption gives sonship now, not merely servant status.

options.text: It is only a figure of speech with no real standing.
options.note: It is a real legal placing into God's family through Christ.

options.text: It means God adopts everyone regardless of Christ.
options.note: The adoption is through Jesus Christ, according to God's will.

quiz.q: How do we have redemption in the Son?

options.text: Through His blood, defined as the forgiveness of our trespasses.
options.note: Verse 7 grounds redemption in Christ's blood and equates it with forgiveness.

options.text: By God simply ignoring our sin at no cost.
options.note: Redemption is by ransom, the blood of Christ, not by overlooking sin.

options.text: By our own good works and religious effort.
options.note: Redemption is in Him, according to the riches of His grace.

options.text: By joining the right spiritual rituals.
options.note: It is through Christ's blood alone, freely given in grace.

quiz.q: What is God's plan for the fullness of time?

options.text: To sum up all things in heaven and on earth under Christ as head.
options.note: Verse 10 reveals the mystery of God's will to gather all things in Christ.

options.text: To rescue souls while abandoning the created world.
options.note: The plan embraces all things in heaven and on earth, not souls only.

options.text: To leave history without any purpose or goal.
options.note: History moves toward the summing up of all things in Christ.

options.text: To exalt the powers of the age above Christ.
options.note: All things are gathered under Christ, not under rival powers.

quiz.q: What role does the Holy Spirit play in verses 13 and 14?

options.text: He seals believers as God's own and is the pledge guaranteeing their inheritance.
options.note: The Spirit is the seal of ownership and the arrabon, the down payment on glory.

options.text: He is a reward given only after a life of good works.
options.note: The Spirit is given when they heard and believed, not earned later.

options.text: He is merely a symbol with no personal presence.
options.note: The seal is a Person, the promised Holy Spirit Himself.

options.text: He replaces the need for any future inheritance.
options.note: He is the pledge of an inheritance still to be fully received.

questions: Paul begins the letter not with commands but with praise for grace. How might starting your own prayers with thanks for what God has already done change the way you pray?
God chose you in Christ before the foundation of the world. How does knowing your salvation rests on His eternal purpose, not your performance, steady you when you feel like a failure?
Adoption means you are a son or daughter with a full inheritance, not a servant hoping to earn a place. Where do you still relate to God as a nervous servant rather than a beloved child?
Redemption came through the blood of Christ, at real cost. How does the price of your forgiveness deepen your sense of how loved you are?
The Spirit is God's down payment, a guarantee of the glory to come. When the future feels uncertain, how does the Spirit's presence now assure you of what is still ahead?

translationNotes.note: Several early manuscripts omit the words in Ephesus, which has led many to think the letter was a circular sent to churches around Ephesus; the BSB retains in Ephesus, as followed here.
In love at the end of verse 4 may modify what precedes, holy and blameless in love, or what follows, in love He predestined; either way it grounds God's choosing in love.
To bring together, anakephalaioo, means to sum up or gather under one head; the BSB renders it together to capture the uniting of all things in Christ.

meta.notes: BSB text for Ephesians 1:1-14 reproduced as supplied. Inline tokens mark the nine supplied lexicon keys, each used once.
